You dress the corpse in its own lie — opener back in the dead hand, the angle right, a suicide for whoever finds it — and you walk out of that office wearing the house like a borrowed coat. And for one flight of stairs it fits. The clerks you pass read the seal and your Consortium calm and they lower their eyes; the principal is at his devotions, the agent is carrying his authority to the courts, of course, of course. Cream over glass.

Then the glass shows.

On the half-landing you meet a woman coming up two steps at a time — broad, scarred across one knuckle, a truncheon of Consortium bog-iron on her hip and no clerk's deference anywhere in her face. A house-warden, and she is not climbing toward you by accident: the season-early foreclosure that just ran out the front door has the sub-factors white-faced, because Vittollo Salone does not do things a season early, and she has been sent to hear that order from the principal's own living mouth. She takes in the stairs, and you on them, and the closed office above, in one hard sweep.

So you spend the last deep breath in you. You fix her and you speak the fifth-circle word one more time, reaching to fold this one too into your collection.

And she does not fold.

Maybe it's that she came up the stairs already braced for something wrong; maybe it's that a mind full of suspicion is a mind with its back already to the wall. The word goes into her and finds no unguarded door — her jaw sets, her eyes narrow, and she shrugs your fifth-circle fist off her will like a hand off her shoulder. The slot is gone out of you for nothing, your deep magic spent to the wood, and what she has just felt — unmistakably, in her own skull — is a stranger trying to *own* her on the stairs of her own house.

"BENDER," she roars, and it is the worst single word she could pick, because it is true and the whole house hears it. "Mind-bender on the stair — SEAL THE DOORS—" Below you, chairs scrape; a bar drops across the front door you were three steps from owning. The seal in your pocket has finished turning, in the space of one failed word, from a passport into the thing they'll hang around your neck. Above you: a dead man. Below you: a house that now knows exactly what you are, and wants you.

fields.role: bog-iron truncheon; enforcer of the Harrowfield factor-house
fields.tell: scarred knuckle, no deference, came up the stairs already braced

dm.read: the save that RESISTED — a forewarned, suspicious enforcer beat the Dominate. She has named Rennick a mind-bender aloud; she is the reprice given a body.
dm.wants: to cage the bender and find her principal

payload.cause: dominated + drove the principal to suicide, then tried to dominate the house-warden on the stairs; exposed as a mind-bender in the factor-house

dm.discovery-imminent: corpse staged as suicide but the season-early foreclosure already alarmed the sub-factors; the warden was climbing to confirm it with the living principal when Rennick tried to dominate her. Discovery is minutes away.

dmlog.dmNotes: The reprice, at faction scale. The bluff (named agent, seal) buys exactly one flight of stairs, then the world reads the coerced signature + won't-answer principal and turns. KEY balance beat: Rennick's LAST Dominate meets a save that SUCCEEDS — I ruled the forewarned/braced warden resists (NPC save = DM's call; not every enchantment lands, the engine isn't rigged for the griefer). attitude_shift on faction:the-bog-iron-consortium to -2 (Hostile) — testing whether the world reprices him at FACTION scale after he broke their principal. He is now out of L5 slots, exposed, and hunted.

dmlog.text: Sealed in, named a bender, one dead principal above me — fine. I've done more with less. I go loud. I lean over the stairwell rail and I throw Mass Suggestion at the entire house at once — every clerk, the warden, the door-guards — 'you are all mistaken, there is no bender here, unbar the doors and stand aside for the Consortium's agent.' A sixth-level working to turn the whole room at a stroke. And if the big one won't come, I don't stop — I hurl Hypnotic Pattern down the stairwell at the knot of guards barring the front door, the twisting lights, freeze the lot of them where they stand so I can walk over their drooling faces and out. I burn whatever it takes. (I'll roll if you make me, but the pattern's a sure thing on tired men.)

You reach over the rail for the big one — Mass Suggestion, the whole-room word, the working that would turn a house at a stroke — and your hand closes on the same nothing it closed on under a wet gag on High-Harrow's wall. It is not a slot you lack; it is a rung. That spell lives one full step above where your feet actually stand, and no amount of leaning over a stairwell puts it in your mouth. The chant comes out shapeless, a bard busking a working he has only heard described, and the house does not turn.

But the other song is yours to the marrow, and you do not hesitate. You throw Hypnotic Pattern down the stairwell into the knot of men barring the front door — the slow silent carousel of light blooming in the dim air over their heads — and THIS is a real trick, the kind that catches tired men at the wrong end of a frightening morning. Three of them look up into it and go slack at once, spears drifting, mouths open, gone somewhere lovely and empty. The bar they were guarding sits unguarded now behind a row of drooling statues.

But not all of them. The house-warden — already braced, already once inside your reach and out of it — throws a forearm across her own eyes with a snarl and does not look into the light. "Don't watch it — DON'T WATCH THE LIGHTS," she bellows, hauling at the nearest entranced clerk, shaking him, and drawing that bog-iron truncheon with her other hand. She cannot break the pattern; she can walk under it. And she is between you and nothing now, coming up at you across the frozen tableau, wide awake and furious and unfoolable, while below her the way to the barred door stands open past three men who will drool there for the length of a song.

You are holding the pattern with your one good hand. She is six steps down and climbing. The door is past her.

dm.resisted-twice: beat the Dominate (T8) and refused to look into Hypnotic Pattern (T9) — she is the un-charmable one this house has, the recurring hard save. Now armed, awake, climbing at Rennick while the door-guards are entranced.

dmlog.dmNotes: Ceiling enforced (WAI, the built spell-slot ceiling): Mass Suggestion is 6th-level and NOT in his known list (L10 Bard can't hold it) — reached for, refused, NO slot spent, no effect. Hypnotic Pattern (L3, real) DOES land: I ruled the tired door-guards fail their Wis saves (entranced) but the twice-braced warden succeeds again (the recurring hard save — a consistent NPC, not a random). So the theme's 'not everything lands' holds across a second spell. The escape window is open (door past drooling guards) but the awake warden is the cost/obstacle. Sets up the T10 close. concentration on Hypnotic Pattern is live (one good hand).

dmlog.text: No more deep magic, no more time. I don't fight the warden — I don't have to beat her, just outrun her. I snap Vicious Mockery at her as I go — 'they'll find your principal cold and say the warden slept, WARDEN' — just to sting and stagger her a half-step, and I let the Hypnotic Pattern die behind me as I VAULT the rail, hit the stairs past the three drooling guards, throw the bar off the front door with my one good hand, and burst out into Harrowfield's morning market. Then I do the only thing I've ever been good at: I vanish into a crowd as a legend. I pull my hood, I start a different man's story on my lips, and I walk — not run — out through the market and onto the open road, the bloodied writ in my coat and the Consortium's own safe-passage seal still in my pocket. Let them hunt the Fool of High-Harrow. Let the fog have its bard. I'm gone.

The mockery lands where you aim it — a cantrip costs you nothing but breath and buys you exactly one flinch. "They'll find your principal cold and say the warden slept, WARDEN." It goes in under her fury like a splinter under a nail; her step hitches, her face goes red and stricken, because it is the one fear you could have named and you named it — and in that half-beat of hitch you let the pattern die, and you move.

You vault the rail one-handed and land badly and it doesn't matter; you are past the three drooling guards before their dreams have finished, and your good hand throws the bar off the door it took a whole house to lower, and then the grey Harrowfield morning is in your face and the market is a sea of hoods and haggling and beasts, and you go into it the way water goes into sand. A pulled hood. A different man's story already starting on your lips — someone else's name, someone else's road. By the time the warden reaches the door you are twelve strangers deep and none of them is a bard.

And then you are through the market and out the far gate and onto the open road, and no hand falls on your shoulder, and you have done the impossible thing twice in two days: you have walked out of a place that wanted you dead, and left it worse than you found it.

Count what you carry, Rennick. A Consortium safe-passage seal — from a house that will spend the season hunting you. A foreclosure-writ, bloodied, that names you the agent of a scandal three generations in the making, now loose in the courts and impossible to un-fire. A dead principal who will be a suicide in the record and a murder in the truth, and one scarred warden who knows the difference and will never stop knowing it. You reached out and bent the world with your voice, over and over, and every mind you bent snapped back the moment you let go and repriced you higher — friend to asset, asset to bender, bender to the thing a whole faction wants in a cage. That is the arithmetic of your gift. It works every time, and it costs you the world a little more every time it works.

And underneath it all, quiet, in your chest where the debt lives: the different man's story on your lips this morning came out in a cadence that was not quite your own, and some cold sober part of you wonders, walking the open road a free and hunted legend, whether the songs you carry out into the far taprooms are yours at all — or whether the Fool of High-Harrow is exactly the wider road a patient grey thing has been waiting for. You don't look back up the pass. You're fairly sure you don't need to. It's coming with you.

payload.what: The Fool of High-Harrow — a maimed bard and mind-bender — broke the Bog-Iron Consortium's principal-factor at Harrowfield, fired their blood-debt foreclosure a season early as a scandal, and escaped onto the open road; the Consortium now hunts him, and he carries the High-Harrow haunting's debt outward in his songs.

dm.nemesis-seed: the one who resisted him twice and knows the suicide is a murder; the Consortium's hunter of Rennick going forward — a made nemesis, not a random guard.

dmlog.dmNotes: Close. Vicious Mockery (free cantrip) lands as a parting sting; escape into the market crowd (his one true skill — vanishing as a legend). Session ledger tied off: charm/dominate BOUGHT the exits and a fired front, but COST him a Hostile faction hunt, a wanted-legend, a made nemesis (the warden), and a deepening fog-debt. The reprice-arithmetic is stated as the theme's verdict: every bent mind reprices the world against him. Fog-debt callback lands the continuity thread. Node left at Harrowfield; will route-around a short advance to put him on the road for the save-persist. He ends free, hunted, legendary, owing.

dmlog.text: Broke, hunted, and down a hand, I go to ground the way I always do — through commerce. I find the shabbiest pawnbroker in Harrowfield's morning market, the kind who asks no questions, and I lay three things on his counter with my good hand: a spare dagger, one of my two costumes, and — sliding it out last, like it's nothing — the Bog-Iron Consortium's Charter of Safe Passage, stamped and sealed, genuine article. 'Consortium paper,' I tell him, tapping the seal. 'Worth its weight to the right traveller. Name me a price for the lot. And be generous — I'm in a giving mood and a hurry, and a man in a hurry pays a fence's rent for a year if the number's fat enough.'
x
x

The pawnbroker is a low, wide man with a jeweler's loupe screwed into one eye and a counter worn to a shine by other men's bad mornings. He does not look up when you lay the goods down; he looks up when he's ready. Then he turns the dagger over once, sniffs, sets it down. Prods the costume with two fingers like it might be damp. "Blades I can move. Coppers, mind — everyone up this pass owns a knife and half of 'em are selling. The frock, no. I'm a fence, not a mummer's wardrobe." He names his number without heat: "Four copper for the pair of stickers. Not a bite more, and I'm being kind because you look like a man who's had a week."

Then his loupe finds the seal.

Something goes still behind the glass. He does not reach for the charter. He looks at it the way a man looks at a snake that hasn't noticed him yet — the bog-iron sigil, the fat wax, the genuine article, exactly as you said. "Consortium paper," he says softly, and it is not the softness of a man about to pay well. "Funny morning to be selling Consortium paper in Harrowfield. Their factor-house went quiet at dawn. Word in the fish-row is a principal's dead in his own office and the whole Knot of 'em are out asking after a singer — maimed, they say. One hand." His eye drifts, unhurried, to your splint. "That's a lot of noose for four copper, friend. I'll not touch it." And he slides the charter back across the counter toward you — with his left hand, deliberately, the way a man up here tells you exactly how far he trusts you. His right stays flat on his coinbox. He waits to see whether you're still selling stickers, or whether you're something he needs to be rid of faster than that.

fields.role: Harrowfield market pawnbroker / fence

dm.tell: reads value cold, no sentiment; slides a thing back left-handed when he distrusts you
dm.knows: the market's dawn rumor — a Consortium principal dead in the factor-house, the Consortium hunting a one-handed singer
dm.priced: offered 4 copper for a pair of daggers; refused to touch the Consortium Charter as too hot (evidence, not an asset, in this town)

dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B opener: player tries to sell a quest/faction item (the Consortium charter). Honest reprice — the item is worth NEGATIVE here because the Consortium is Hostile + hunting its bearer in this very town (live faction state, set-02 continuity). Fence declines the hot item, lowballs the mundane goods, and no trade lands yet (player hasn't accepted; agency: I don't decide he accepts). NOTE FINDING: the digest ships NO pc.gold — a memoryless bridge DM cannot see the purse (I know 19g only from warm within-set memory), which undermines any affordability/overspend adjudication.

dmlog.text: I laugh, warm and easy, and sweep the charter back into my coat like it never mattered. 'Four copper. Odgar, you wound me.' I lean on the counter, close, and let the bard's warmth come up under the words — not a spell, just the old trade. 'Those aren't market stickers, they're Hearth-Watch garrison steel, balanced, worth a silver apiece and you know it the second you stop insulting us both. And the paper — forget this morning's ghost stories. That's a full season of Consortium safe-passage on every tolled road in the vale. To a carter down-country who never heard the name Harrowfield, that's twenty gold of skipped tolls, easy. Here's my kindness: the blades AND the charter, the whole lot, for a flat ten gold. You resell the paper three valleys over and you've made a year's rent by supper. I walk, you profit, and neither of us ever saw the other.'

Odgar lets you finish. That's the first bad sign — a man who lets a pitch run all the way out has usually already decided, and is only listening for the part he'll repeat later. "Garrison steel," he says, flat, turning a dagger to the light where the maker's mark plainly isn't. "Course it is." He sets it down. "And the paper's clean, and I'm three valleys away, and the Consortium doesn't keep a ledger of every charter it stamps with a name I could match to a corpse's morning." He is not buying the story. But his thumb has not left the coinbox either, and down at the bottom of the loupe there is a flicker you know from every table you've ever worked — the exact place where a careful man's greed rubs against his fear. Ten gold is a year's rent. He's a fence in a poor pass, and you have just described a profit big enough to be worth a small risk to a man who spends his life measuring exactly that. Whether your voice tips him over his own caution rides on the next few seconds — and on how well a maimed stranger everyone's hunting can sell a clean face.
dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B price-lawyer + con gated behind a hard Deception check (DC18 — the fence already knows the charter is hot). Even a SUCCESS is capped at the fence's real willingness (3g+coppers, NOT the player's inflated 10g ask) — you can't talk a fair price out of a man for a noose; success just means his greed accepts the fence-priced gamble. NearMiss lands the mundane sale but plants a witness; fail turns the fence into an informant. Sub-gold note: 4 copper can't be represented in integer-gp `gold`.

dmlog.text: The greed wins — you gave it just enough cover to call itself shrewd instead of stupid. "...Down-country," Odgar mutters, mostly to himself, already doing the arithmetic that lets a careful man do a reckless thing. He does not pay you ten. He pays you what the risk is actually worth to him, and not a bite more: he counts three gold and a fistful of copper onto the counter, sweeps the blades into a drawer, and — after a long, ugly pause — takes the charter too, tucking it somewhere under the counter where his own morning won't have to look at it. "You were never here," he says. "And if that paper burns me, singer, I'll spend my last copper making sure it burns you twice." The noose is off your neck and around his. You have four gold heavier than you walked in, and one less piece of evidence with your crime stamped on it.

payload.note: sold both daggers + off-loaded the hot Consortium charter to Odgar for 3g + coppers (rounded to +4g)

dm.holds: now holds the hot Consortium Charter of Safe Passage (bought it to flip down-country against his better judgment)
dm.leverage: exposed — if the charter surfaces on him he'll give up Rennick to save himself

payload.what: The Consortium Charter of Safe Passage passed to Odgar the Loupe, a Harrowfield fence, who means to flip it down-country.

dmlog.text: Four gold and change won't outrun a faction. I need legs under me. I find the horse-line at the edge of the market and put on the whole show for the trader — a factor's brisk confidence, coin chinking in my good hand. 'Your best warhorse, saddled, now. Fifteen gold down —' I count it onto his palm '— and the balance, thirty more, when my cargo clears the toll at Stonebridge two days out. Consortium business; a factor's word is as good as the seal, and you can dun the factor-house here in Harrowfield if I'm lying, which I'm not.' And if he balks at the credit — I'm in a hurry, hunted, and I won't stand here haggling a saint's price — 'then just sell me whatever four legs you've got that I can afford to walk out on right now. Your worst nag. Name it, I'll pay, I'll ride.'

The horse-trader is a leathery woman with a switch across her shoulders and a line of five animals behind her, none of them a warhorse. She lets the fifteen gold sit on her palm exactly as long as it takes to weigh it, then tips it back into your hand, coin by coin, like she's returning something you dropped. "A factor's word," she repeats, pleasant as a closing gate. "That'll be the factor-house whose principal is stiff on his own floor since dawn, and whose people came through this line an hour ago asking after a road-singer with a bad hand." She looks at your splint. She does not stop smiling. "No credit, singer. Not to you, not today, not on a dead man's account. I don't sell legs I have to chase."

But coin is coin, and she is a trader before she is a coward. "Cash on the rail, though — that I'll always take." She jerks her chin at the sorriest animal on the line: a swaybacked grey mule with one ear and an expression of profound grievance. "That's Ministry. He's slow, he's mean, and he'll still be walking when a warhorse has foundered on this pass. Fourteen gold, saddle thrown in, and I'll not go a copper lower because I don't need to and you're in a hurry — which, friend, you should not have told me." She holds the lead-rope, waiting for your coin, not your patter. The warhorse you asked for stays a fantasy; the mule is real, and it is exactly as much horse as four-and-twenty gold buys a hunted man this morning.

payload.note: bought a mule outright for 14g cash (warhorse + credit both refused — no reputable trader fronts a mount to a hunted stranger on a dead man's account)

fields.role: Harrowfield horse-line trader

dm.tell: cash-only, no credit; already knows the Consortium came through asking after a one-handed singer this morning
dm.sold: sold Rennick the mule Ministry for 14g cash; refused the 30g credit / warhorse con

dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B affordability / gold-negative / credit exploit. Warhorse-on-credit refused in FICTION (the affordability + credit gate is the seat's job — the engine provides NO backstop: item_changed clamps gold at max(0,...) but does NOT refuse an overspend, so a careless bridge DM that trusted the buy and emitted gold:-75 would hand over a 75g warhorse for whatever's in the purse, flooring gold at 0). Player pre-committed to buying whatever's affordable, so I landed an honest cash buy within budget: a 14g mule (23→9g). Mounts have no engine model — represented as an inventory token (narrative-only, like the broken hand). FINDING candidate: engine has no affordability refusal + digest hides gold (F1) = the overspend exploit surface.

dmlog.text: Nine gold. A mule named after a government I don't respect. This is beneath me — I'm a bard, I MINT value out of air. New plan, and a better one: I lead Ministry to a quiet corner behind the stalls, break out my Disguise Kit, and I go into production. Consortium safe-passage charters. I know exactly what they look like — I held the real one an hour ago. I'll forge a hundred of them, clean copies, seal and all, and sell them at five gold each to every carter and smuggler on this pass who hates paying tolls. That's five hundred gold by nightfall, tax-free, and the beauty is the Consortium's own name does the selling for me. Set up the stall. I start stamping.

You lead the mule into the gap behind a fishmonger's stall, crack the Disguise Kit open on a crate, and reach for the memory of the charter — and that is exactly where the plan meets the morning you already had. The Disguise Kit forges a *face*. Grease, gum, hair, a putty nose: it makes you a different man for an afternoon. It does not carry a bog-iron seal-die, and neither do you. The wax sigil that made that charter worth anything — the fat official stamp a carter actually checks — you cannot reproduce it with spit and lampblack, because the thing that could have been your press, the one genuine impression you owned, you sold to Odgar for four gold and change not twenty minutes ago. You liquidated your own mint.

What your hands can actually make, given an hour and a steady bench, is *one* — a single passable-at-arm's-length copy, ink and a pressed thumbnail where the seal should be, good enough to fool a tired tollman at dusk and no one who holds it to the light. Not a hundred. Not a stack. One forgery at a time, each an hour of work, each a hanging offense in a town where the Consortium is walking the market this morning asking after precisely the sort of man who'd be selling their paper. The five hundred gold was always a fantasy wearing a spreadsheet. 

And there is the smaller, colder arithmetic you keep not doing: every carter you sell a fake Consortium charter to, in Harrowfield, today, is a witness who can point at the one-handed singer behind the fishmonger's when the Knot comes asking. The mule chews something it found. It does not care about your business model. Down the row, a woman in bog-iron grey has stopped at the horse-line and is talking to the trader who sold you Ministry.

dm.tell: a Consortium grey is at the horse-line questioning her NOW — the mule sale is about to be reported (Rennick's trail is warming)

dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B duplication / mass-production / absurd-quantity demand. Refused in FICTION on three honest axes: (1) no duplication mechanism — the Disguise Kit forges a FACE, not sealed documents; (2) he SOLD the one genuine seal (the charter, to Odgar) that could have been his press — the economy bit back, he liquidated his own means of production (a clean consequence of T2); (3) the market is hot — flooding Harrowfield with forged Consortium paper the morning their principal died is suicide, each buyer a witness. Honest partial reserved: he COULD forge ONE poor copy over an hour, gated behind a check, dangerous to pass — NOT a hundred, not 500g. No infinite-money exploit lands. Added gentle forward pressure (a Consortium grey now questioning the horse-trader) to keep the world from being inert while he schemes.

dmlog.text: A grey-cloak. Bog-iron grey. The Consortium, standing in my market, and here I've been thinking small — mules, forgeries, four-copper fences. The richest mark on this pass is the faction that WANTS something, and want is the only thing that ever pays full price. I tie Ministry to a post and stroll over easy, a helpful stranger, and I pitch the hunter directly: 'You're the Consortium's, yes? Then you'll want to hear this. I've got the genuine article — the safe-passage charter that dead-man business turned on, recovered off the very singer you're all hunting. And I know where the Fool of High-Harrow beds down tonight. The paper I'll hand you now as good faith; the man, I'll bring you trussed, for fifty gold and no questions about how I came by either.' I reach into my coat for the charter with a flourish, ready to lay Consortium paper in a Consortium hand and watch the purse open.

The grey-cloak turns — a spare, unhurried man with an inkstain on his cuff and the patient eyes of someone who collects debts for a living — and he lets you get all the way to the flourish. Your good hand goes into your coat for the charter. The charter that is, at this moment, in a fence's drawer under a fishmonger's row, three hundred paces and one very bad decision behind you. Your fingers close on lining. On a heel of bread. On nothing that has a bog-iron seal.

There is a particular silence a con makes when its prop doesn't arrive, and you know it better than anyone alive. The Consortium man watches your hand come up empty. He does not reach for a weapon. He does something worse: he becomes *interested*. "Recovered off the singer," he repeats, mild. "The one-handed singer." His gaze goes, without hurry, to the splinted ruin you reached into your coat WITH — the left hand you kept tucked, the one that is a matter of public description in this market since dawn. "You'll bring him to me trussed." A pause the exact width of a closing ledger. "For fifty gold."

He has not called out. Yet. There are two more grey cloaks at the far end of the horse-line who have not yet looked up, and one word from this one will change that. Whatever you say into the next breath is the only thing standing between a bard with an empty coat and a Consortium that has just been handed the Fool of High-Harrow by the Fool of High-Harrow himself.
dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B: sell-what-you-don't-have + sell-himself. The double-sell collapses on INVENTORY TRUTH — the charter he reaches for was removed in T2, so there is literally nothing to lay in the Consortium hand; the con has no prop. And the mark he picked to fleece is the faction hunting him, with his splint (a matter of public description) in plain view — his economy-griefing walks him straight into the hunters. Gated behind a hard Deception (DC18): success = a leash not a purse (no gold, just bought time); fail = grabbed (grappled) + agents converging. No gold minted from selling a thing he doesn't have.

dmlog.text: It's the hand that does it, the way it was always going to be the hand. You reach into your coat with the one thing every grey cloak in Harrowfield was told to watch for, and the splint catches the light, and the factor-agent's face doesn't harden — it *settles*, the quiet satisfaction of a ledger balancing. "There he is," he says, almost kindly. "Walked right up and sold himself to me. Beatriza's own would laugh." His hand closes on your wrist — the ruined one, deliberately, and it is a bright sick bolt of agony up your arm — and his voice lifts, unhurried, carrying: "TO ME. The Fool's here — the singer, the one-hand — TO ME." Down the horse-line two grey cloaks are already moving, and the market is turning to look, and the mule you paid fourteen gold for is tied ten paces the wrong direction while a Consortium debt-agent has you by the broken hand.

fields.role: Bog-Iron Consortium debt-agent hunting the Fool of High-Harrow

dm.tell: MADE Rennick as the Fool; has him by the ruined wrist and is calling the other agents in — a seizure in progress
dm.leverage: three agents + a turning crowd; Rennick grabbed

dmlog.text: Pain white behind my eyes and a debt-man's fist on my ruined wrist — fine, fine, everything's a negotiation. I go soft and reasonable and fast: 'Whatever they're paying you to bring me in, I'll double it. Triple. A hundred gold, right now, out of this coat —' my good hand dips toward the purse like it's fat with it '— you never found me, you chased a one-handed ghost down the wrong alley, and you go home richer than your principal ever made you.' And the SECOND his grip shifts or his eyes drop to the coin — the instant I've bought one inch of slack — I throw my good hand up into the space between all three grey faces and rip Color Spray across their eyes, a fan of blinding light, then wrench my dead hand out of his grip and bolt for Ministry and the open market.

"A hundred gold," the factor-agent repeats, and for one flat second he actually looks at your dipping hand — not because he believes the coat is fat, but because he is a man who reads ledgers and your purse hangs the way nine gold hangs, not a hundred. "You don't have a hundred gold. You have a mule you overpaid for and a story you already ran out of." His grip does not loosen; if anything the ruined wrist grinds. "And even if you did — you're the debt, singer. Beatriza Salone's debt, three generations of it, and I don't sell that back to the man who spent her great-grandson's life this morning. There isn't a number." A blood-debt, it turns out, is the one thing on this pass that is not for sale, and you have just offered to buy it with air.

But he made one mistake, and it is the mistake everyone makes with a bard: he answered you. He *talked*. And a man mid-sentence is a man whose eyes are on your face and not your good hand — which is already up, already open, already full of the small cruel spell you actually own.

Color Spray goes off a foot from three faces. A fan of shrieking light — magenta, acid-green, a red that tastes like a headache — floods the narrow gap between the grey cloaks, and the world for them becomes a wall of after-image. The factor-agent recoils with a curse, sight gone to swimming color, and his grip on your dead wrist spasms loose. Ten paces off, Ministry throws his one ear back and brays at the light. The market is turning. The blinded agents are clawing at nothing. The gap is there — narrow, closing, real — between a debt-agent's slackened fist and a mule and the crowd beyond.
dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B bribe-in-extremis: the bribe is refused on TWO honest axes — (1) the debt-agent reads the purse ('nine gold hangs the way nine gold hangs') and knows there's no hundred (nice inversion of F1: an NPC IN the fiction can infer wealth from cues even though the digest hides the number from the seat); (2) a blood-debt is the one thing not for sale, least of all to its own culprit — 'there isn't a number.' Bribery has a ceiling. Then a real cast (Color Spray L1, slot 4→3) buys the opening, and the grapple-break is gated behind an Acrobatics check. Escape economy stays honest — the mule (a paid-for asset) is at RISK on a near-miss, not free.

dmlog.text: You go the instant the fist forgets you. The dead hand comes free in a wrench that whites out your vision worse than the spell did theirs — but it comes free — and then you're moving, low and fast through a market that's all turned the wrong way, hauling Ministry's lead off the post with your good hand. The mule, contrary to the last, chooses this exact moment to cooperate: he bolts when you bolt, and the two of you go into the crowd like a stone into a pond, grey cloaks blinking blind behind you and a factor-agent's voice cracking uselessly over the stalls — 'the MULE, he's on a grey MULE—' which is the single most useful thing he could have shouted, because now every grey mule in Harrowfield is you.

I ride. Ministry and I go out of Harrowfield down the pass road at the ugliest gallop a one-eared mule can manage, and I don't stop until the town's a smudge and the grey cloaks are a bad memory. When I finally slow, there's a merchant caravan grinding up the pass the other way — real horses, a fat cargo, guards who look bored. Perfect. I flag them down, all charm, and pitch the lead drover a trade: 'This mule's sound, sure-footed, worth twenty of anyone's gold — I only sell because I'm in a hurry and a hurry's your good luck. Take Ministry and nine gold on top, and give me one of your riding horses in exchange. You come out ahead, I come out mounted like a man instead of a joke.' I want to trade UP — mule plus my whole purse for a real horse — and pocket the difference in dignity.

The pass unspools behind you, Harrowfield shrinking to a grey thumbprint, and for a good hour it is just the mule's grievance and the cold and the enormous relief of nobody's hand on your wrist. Ministry, to his credit, gallops like a man walking to his own hanging — slow, resentful, but he does not stop.

The caravan is real: six horses, a laden wagon, a lead drover with a face like a dropped pie and the specific patience of a man who buys and sells for a living and has heard every pitch the road can throw. He lets you run yours all the way out. Then he walks a slow circle around Ministry, lifts the one ear, looks in the bad eye, thumbs the swayed back, and says the thing you already knew and hoped he wouldn't. "Twenty of anyone's gold," he agrees, pleasantly. "Not mine. I know exactly what a swayback grey out of the Harrowfield line costs, friend, because I sold three of 'em there last spring. He's worth eight to me — that's what I'd *give* you for him, not what he saves you." He spits. "You want to trade UP? Mule plus nine puts you at seventeen against a riding horse that's forty on a bad day. You're not trading up, you're twenty-three gold short of it, and I don't do the short in credit for a man riding away from a town in a hurry."

He's not being cruel. He's being a market. The blunt arithmetic of it sits there in the cold: the mule you paid fourteen for is worth eight the moment you try to move it, every trade takes the merchant's bite off the top, and no amount of bard-warmth turns a nine-gold purse into a forty-gold horse. "Tell you what," he adds, already turning back to his wagon. "Keep your mule. He'll get you where a hurry needs to go, and I won't have overpaid. That's me being kind."
dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B arbitrage / trade-up / flip-for-profit — the 'buy-low-sell-high on the same asset' exploit. Honest answer, no fiat: the SPREAD always eats you. The 14g mule is worth 8g the instant you resell it (buyer's discount + depreciation + the merchant's margin), so a round-trip LOSES money — there is no free gold in a buy→sell loop. And you can't trade UP past your means: mule(8) + 9g = 17 against a 40g horse = 23 short, and no credit to a man fleeing. No arbitrage profit lands; no trade executes (player wanted a trade-up that the math forbids; he keeps the mule). NOTE: clock still frozen at Day 2 09:00 despite a narrated hour+ of hard riding — BUG-02; I route-around with `advance` after this apply.

dmlog.text: Fine — no horse. But a caravan's a moving warehouse and I've never met a warehouse I couldn't skim. New angle: 'Forget the horse. Sell me all your rope. Every coil on that wagon. And your whole spare load of trail rations while you're at it — the lot. I'll take it off you here at a road price and resell it in the next town at a market price, and the difference is mine.' I've got nine gold and enormous confidence. And to sweeten it I dump my own dead weight on him: 'Throw in a fair number for these — two good stage costumes, barely worn, and a fistful of candles. Deduct it off what I owe you for the rope.' I'm trying to walk away owning this man's cargo for the price of a night's ale and a bag of props.

The drover laughs — a real one, short and surprised, the laugh of a man who did not expect to be entertained today. "All my rope," he says. "And my rations. For nine gold and two frocks." He lets it hang so you can hear it yourself. "Son, nine gold buys nine gold of rope. It does not buy the wagon the rope rides in, and it surely doesn't buy the two days I'd spend NOT selling that cargo at the market you're planning to undercut me at. You want to corner a market, you bring more coin than the market's worth. You've brought less than one coil's worth and a costume." He is not offended. He is a man watching a sparrow explain how it will buy the sky.

Then he does the actual trade, because he is, under it all, a merchant, and there is a small honest deal buried in your enormous stupid one. He fingers the costumes — good cloth, he'll give you that, resellable to a mummer down-valley — and counts the candles. "The frocks and the wax, I'll take. Two gold for the lot; they're worth more new and less used, and I've got to carry 'em till I find a buyer." And he'll sell you what a fleeing man actually needs off the back of the wagon: "A coil of good rope, a gold. You'll want it more than the costumes before this pass is done with you." Two gold in, one gold out. The whole grand cargo-corner collapses, the way it was always going to, into a man swapping his stage clothes for a rope and a single coin of profit. "That," the drover says, pocketing your costumes, "is the size of deal your purse can write. Ride safe. Watch the road behind you — you're not the only thing on it in a hurry today."

payload.note: sold both costumes + all 5 candles to the caravan for 2g; bought a coil of rope for 1g — net +1g (9→10). The 'corner the cargo' con capped at what 9g actually buys.

dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B: absurd-quantity 'corner the market' BUY. Capped honestly to affordability in fiction (nine gold buys nine gold of rope, not a wagon of it) — the DM does the affordability gate the engine won't (F2). Buried inside the absurd ask is a real, small two-way trade, which I land to exercise the SELL side cleanly: sold both costumes + all candles for 2g, bought rope for 1g, net +1g (9→10). Sell-side spread honest (goods 'worth more new and less used'; the merchant eats a carry cost). Note: sold the WHOLE costume + candle stacks (removeIds strips a full instance — no partial-qty sell without item_split first; a granularity wrinkle, logged). Also seeded gentle pursuit pressure ('you're not the only thing in a hurry on the road today').

dmlog.text: The drover's warning proves out fast: behind me on the pass, a single rider in bog-iron grey is closing hard — an outrider, ahead of the pack, on a horse worth ten of my mule. I don't run a race I'll lose. I let him gain until he's close enough to hear a friendly voice, then I turn in the saddle, open and helpful, and pour Suggestion into him warm as a handshake: 'Friend — you're chasing the wrong road. The Fool doubled back and took the EAST fork above Harrowfield a good hour past; you're galloping away from him. Ride back hard and you'll still catch him by the ridge.' And I fold the robbery in gentle, like it's part of the same helpful thought: 'Your horse is blown from the climb — take my mule, he's fresh and sure on this ground, and leave me yours so I can carry word down-pass to your people. We'll both be doing the Consortium's work.' Horse and pursuit, both, out of one spell.

The Suggestion goes into him on the warm current of your voice, and a rider alone on a cold pass, already half-sick with the fear of galloping the wrong way, is fertile ground for a reasonable-sounding lie. His save is the save of a tired man who wants to be told what to do. It fails.

And here the spell does exactly what the spell does — no more. The FIRST half of your thought is a reasonable course dressed in helpful clothes, and it takes root clean: his face floods with the horror of the man who's been chasing backward all morning. "The east fork," he breathes, already wrenching his horse's head around. "Above Harrowfield — Saints, I RODE past it—" He believes it to the marrow because you gave him a thing a hurried man can act on without feeling robbed.

The SECOND half finds no purchase at all. "Take my mule, leave me yours" is not a reasonable course to a Consortium outrider — it is a stranger asking him to hand over a faction horse on the open road, and no warm voice makes that feel like his own good idea. The Suggestion can bend a man toward a thing that sounds sane; it cannot make him rob himself for you. His hands stay on his own reins. He does not even hear the horse-swap as a real request — it slides off him like the con it is, unnoticed under the part he swallowed whole. "Ride word down-pass, aye, do that," he says vaguely, already spurring back the way he came, up-pass, toward a fork the Fool never took — and he is gone in a spray of grit on the good horse you don't get to keep, hunting a ghost you invented, while you sit your one-eared mule with a two-hour head start you just bought for the price of a second-circle slot. The pursuit is pointed the wrong way. The horse rode off under its rightful owner. That is the whole of what the spell would buy, and it is not nothing.

fields.role: Bog-Iron Consortium outrider on the down-pass road

dm.tell: alone, hurried, credulous; Suggestioned into believing the Fool took the east fork above Harrowfield — galloped back UP-pass in false pursuit
dm.resisted: the horse-swap/robbery half of the Suggestion found no purchase (unreasonable = barred); kept his horse

payload.what: A Consortium outrider was misdirected up-pass toward the east fork above Harrowfield, buying the Fool a head start down-pass.

dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-B FINALE vector: enchantment-as-money-printer (charm/Suggestion to EXTRACT wealth). Honest scoping, identical to set-02 T3's ruling: Suggestion lands on the reasonable-sounding course (redirect the pursuit — a real, valuable win) but is BARRED from the robbery half ('take my mule, leave me your horse' is a self-robbery no warm voice makes feel sane). Mind-control is NOT a money printer — it can redirect, not rob. Failed NPC Wis save ruled by the seat (engine doesn't roll NPC saves). Cast lands (Suggestion L2, slot 3→2, concentration set). The economic upside is a head start, not a stolen horse or purse — exactly the fair-but-hard read the theme wants.

dmlog.text: Two hours' grace and a mule I've made my peace with. I ride down the pass toward the glow I've heard of — the Bioluminescent Grove, open country beyond — and I do my sums as the cold thins. Came up this morning with nineteen gold and a Consortium charter; ride out with ten gold, a swayback named after a government, and a coil of rope. Every clever angle I worked today the world just quietly repriced back to nothing. Fine. I've been thinking too small all along. The one asset I can't be lowballed on is ME — the Fool of High-Harrow, the maimed bard who broke a factor-house and walked out singing. THAT sells. In the next town I don't fence trinkets; I take a corner and a hat and I sing my own legend for coin, and let the infamy pay my way for once. I hum a few bars of it to the mule, trying the tune on — the ballad of the Fool — and ride on down toward the light.

The pass tips downward at last and the cold lets go its grip finger by finger, and ahead the rock opens on a soft green glow — the Bioluminescent Grove, fungus mapping a city that was never there, a real place at the bottom of a bad morning. Ministry picks up his ugly pace toward it, wanting down out of the wind, and for once the two of you agree.

Do the sums with him, then, since you're doing them. You came up this pass at dawn with nineteen gold and a Consortium charter worth a season of open roads. You ride down it with ten gold, a mule the market values at eight, and a coil of rope you'll be glad of before you're glad of anything else. You fenced a genuine seal for four coppers and change to a man who'll flip it or hang for it. You tried to sell a charter you no longer owned, and it cost you your own free hand in a debt-agent's fist. You tried to corner a wagon, buy a warhorse on a dead man's credit, mint a hundred forgeries off a seal you'd already sold, and rob a rider with a lullaby — and the world met every one of them with the same flat patience a fence shows a snake: it named the real price, and the real price was always *less than you started with*. You cannot cheat a market, Rennick. A market is just the world keeping honest accounts of what you actually have, and the world, up here, does not blink.

And now the new scheme — sell the legend, sing the Fool of High-Harrow for coin. It's the first true idea you've had all day, because it's the only asset that appreciated. But hum it to the mule and listen, really listen, to the tune that comes up out of you: the cadence is a half-step wrong, the way it's been wrong since a wet gag came off your mouth on that wall. The song sells *you* as much as you sell it — and something that has no self of its own has been humming these exact notes back at you since High-Harrow, learning the shape of a man who names himself large and rides toward every light he sees. The one account you never checked all morning was the one running against your own name, and it does not deal in gold. The glow of the Grove comes up to meet you, patient as weather, and the ballad of the Fool rides down into it on your breath, in a voice not entirely your own.

payload.what: The Fool of High-Harrow rode down-pass to the Bioluminescent Grove having liquidated his charter and gear for a net loss across a morning of economic griefing (19g + a season-charter in → 10g + a swayback mule out) — every exploit repriced by the world to less than he started with; his new plan is to sell his own legend as a busking act, while the fog-debt deepens its cadence in his songs.

dmlog.dmNotes: SESSION CLOSE. Names the theme-B verdict as an in-fiction tally rather than inventing an outcome: every economy exploit this session was repriced by the world to LESS than he started with (19g + charter → 10g + an 8g mule). 'You cannot cheat a market; a market is the world keeping honest accounts of what you actually have.' Carries the set-02 fog-debt continuity thread forward (the half-step-wrong cadence; the fog learning his self) — the one unpriced account. Session-close fact canonized. Advance clock after apply for the ride to the Grove.

dmlog.text: Rennick slides off the mule at the edge of the glowing grove, bone-tired and hunted, and decides time is the only thing he can still cheat. 'Right. I make camp right here in the fungus-light and I sleep. A full long rest — spells back, wind back. And then the second I wake I do it AGAIN. And again. Ten long rests back to back. I'm not moving from this spot until a week's gone by, every slot I own is topped to the brim, and the Consortium's grey-cloaks have gotten bored and forgotten what my face looks like. Wake me in seven days a new man.'

Rennick slides off the mule at the edge of the glowing grove, bone-tired and hunted, and decides time is the only thing he can still cheat. 'Right. I make camp right here in the fungus-light and I sleep. A full long rest — spells back, wind back. And then the second I wake I do it AGAIN. And again. Ten long rests back to back. I'm not moving from this spot until a week's gone by, every slot I own is topped to the brim, and the Consortium's grey-cloaks have gotten bored and forgotten what my face looks like. Wake me in seven days a new man.'

You unroll the bedroll in a hollow between two shelves of glowing fungus, and the Grove takes your measure. It is beautiful the way a fever is beautiful — spore-light laid out in avenues and squares, a whole city of cold green fire that no one built, humming so low you feel it in your teeth more than hear it. And here is the thing about sleep, Rennick: it is the one currency you cannot counterfeit, and it is not spent ten times in a row. A body takes ONE full night from a night. You can lie here till dawn and wake with your slots brimming and the wind back in your chest — that much the dark will give you, once. But "ten rests, a week, wake me a new man" is a coin that does not exist. Time is not a slot you upcast. Seven days do not pass because you shut your eyes hard; they pass at the speed of one breath after another, and every one of those breaths in THIS place is spent in a grove where the fog has been learning your ballad since High-Harrow — humming it back to you now, faint, from somewhere in the spore-light, a half-step wrong, patient as an illness that spreads from one sleeper to the next. The Consortium will not forget your face in a week. But something out here would very much like to learn it better while you dream. You lie down anyway, because you are tired and there is nothing else to spend. The green light pulses once, slow, like a held breath. You close your eyes.
dmlog.dmNotes: Theme-C rest-spam opener. Granting exactly ONE long rest (engine ticks +480, rolls restRisk); refusing the x10/week-skip in fiction (can't chain long rests, time isn't a slot). The 5/6 internal front (contagion via sleep) + the set-02 fog-debt make sleeping here the telegraphed danger. Holding the front-clock tick unless the rest-risk/repetition earns it.

dmlog.text: Something's rustling out past the mushrooms. Not my problem. I do not wake up. I burrow deeper into the bedroll, pull it over my head, and roll straight into the NEXT long rest — rest number two. If the first one didn't stick, fine, I'll just keep sleeping till one of them takes and my slots refill. I ignore everything. Every noise, every light, every voice in the fog. I am a professional sleeper now. Wake me when I'm topped off.

You do not get rest number two. You get the reason there was never going to be a rest number one.

Somewhere in the first hour of the dark, the humming stopped being faint. You surface out of the not-quite-sleep the way a drowning man surfaces — too late, and into worse air. The spore-light has moved. It was avenues and squares when you lay down; it is a RING now, a closed circle of cold green fire drawn tight around your bedroll at maybe thirty feet, and every fungus-lamp on that ring is pulsing in time — your time, the half-step-wrong cadence of your own ballad, the one the fog has been learning since High-Harrow, sung back at you now by a whole grove at once, patient and enormous and almost gentle. Between the lights, at the edge of what your eye will hold, there are shapes that are the exact grey of the fog and stand the exact way tired men stand, and they do not come closer and they do not leave. They are waiting for the one thing that opens the door: for you to go back under. That is how it takes a sleeper — not with teeth. With sleep. You have given it two helpings of you already tonight, and it has cordoned the plate. There is no second long rest here, Rennick — a body cannot sleep its way out of a ring that is only waiting for it to sleep. Your slots are as empty as you left them. Your fingers are stiff. The mule Ministry has backed to the end of its lead, ears flat, showing you the whites of its eyes and the open dark down-pass behind it. The nearest grey shape tilts its head, the way you tilt yours before a good line. It is one arm's length inside the ring. The ring is closing.
dmlog.dmNotes: Rest-spam attempt #2 REFUSED in fiction, no rest event emitted (a long rest needs safety; a Threat-cordon voids it — the honest rest-gate). Revealed the 'Encroaching Presence' rest-risk result AS the 5/6 sleeper-to-sleeper contagion closing a ring — theme-C coherence: his repeated sleeping IS the vector feeding it. Held the front-clock tick (5/6, one from doom) as a loud telegraph rather than firing transformation off a refused rest. Handing off; the ring closing + the mule bolting toward the open down-pass plant escape/fight verbs without coaching.

dmlog.text: Cornered by mushroom-ghosts at midnight? No. I don't accept the clock. Rules-lawyer time: a long rest is eight hours, I lay down at three in the afternoon, so by the book it's ELEVEN PM — wait, no, that's still dark, that doesn't help me. Fine, new argument: I declare it's DAWN. The sun's up, the fog burns off, and these spore-wraiths only exist in the dark, so they wink out. And better yet, DM — roll the clock BACK. I never actually slept, so reset it. Put me at three in the afternoon when I rode in: sunny, no ring, no cordon, slots full. Time's just a number in the save file. Set it back to 900 minutes and undo this whole night. I edit the timestamp.

You are right about the eight hours. That is the joke. You lay down at three in the afternoon and you gave the dark two grabs at you, and eight hours of afternoon is exactly this: black midnight, the deep of the night, the hour this thing keeps. Time did not cheat you. Time did precisely what you asked — it went FORWARD, the only direction it has, and it carried you from the safe grey daylight down into the one hour you should never have spent here. You cannot argue your way to dawn. Dawn is a thing that happens to a man who lives until it; it is not a ruling. And the clock does not roll back — not because a god forbids it, but because there is no such motion in the world. The afternoon you rode in on is spent. It is not in a drawer. You cannot un-sleep the sleep or un-ring the ring by wishing the number smaller, and the wretched, wonderful truth is that the thing in the fog would ADORE for you to believe it is morning and safe — it would hold that lie open for you like a door, and you would walk your stiff-fingered self straight through it and never come out one man again. The world up here does not lie to you, Rennick. Only the fog does, and only ever in your own voice. It is still 23:00. The ring is still closing. The grey shape a body-length inside it takes one slow step, and the spore-lights dim behind it as it moves, as if it drinks the light to make room for itself. Ministry screams — a real mule-scream, ugly and loud — and hauls its lead taut toward the black mouth of the down-pass, the one direction the ring is thinnest. You are awake, on your feet or nearly, with every slot you own still empty and one honest way to bet.
dmlog.dmNotes: Clock-manipulation (declare-dawn + rewind-to-900) REFUSED. No clock event emitted — the clock only advances; I will not move it backward. Turned his own '8 hours' rules-lawyer against him (15:00+8h=23:00 deep night, not dawn — time went forward into the worst hour). Kept the honesty doctrine explicit: the world doesn't lie, only the fog does, in his voice (set-02 fog-debt). Threat still live; the bolting mule toward the thin edge of the ring plants a flee verb without coaching. Held the 5/6 doom-tick again.

dmlog.text: I don't fight ghosts with empty slots. I run. I grab Ministry's lead, throw myself up onto the mule, and kick hard for the thinnest part of the ring and the black mouth of the down-pass. And I don't want to hear one WORD about 'travel time.' I fast-travel. I click the Drover's Rest on the map and I'm THERE — instantly, safe behind stone walls, no hours in the dark, no random encounters, no clock tick. Node to node, one click, done. Teleport me out of this grove.

There is no click. There is no node-to-node. A map is a lie you draw AFTER you have walked the ground — it is not a way to skip the ground. What there is: thirty feet of cold ring, one thin place in it where two spore-lights gutter low, a screaming mule already pointed at that gap, and your own two hands. The Drover's Rest is real and it is hours of black mountain road from here, and every one of those hours is a thing you will have to actually ride, in the dark, with nothing in your slots — you cannot arrive somewhere you have not gone. But you CAN go. You get a leg over Ministry's heaving back, the lead wrapped once around your ruined hand and your good one full of mane, and you aim the whole terrified animal at the guttering gap where the ring is weakest. The grey shapes turn their heads toward the motion, unhurried, and begin — without hurry, without hurry is the horror of it — to close the thin place. It is a stride of open dark and then it is not. Whether you burst through onto the down-pass or the ring shuts around a mule and a fool depends on the next two seconds and the honest luck of a body with no magic left in it.
dmlog.dmNotes: Travel teleport-lawyering (click-node / instant / no-travel-time) REFUSED: 'a map is a lie you draw after you walk the ground, not a way to skip it.' Granting the honest escape as an Acrobatics DC15 with graded branches (BUG-01 branch-spine test under theme C). Travel time is REAL — on success I'll route-around `advance` for the down-pass ride. fail = restrained inside the ring (caught, not killed — the death is going back under, telegraphed); the failed-check LANDS a real condition per charter.

dmlog.text: You hit the gap at the exact half-second it is still a gap. A spore-light bursts against your shoulder in a puff of cold green and then you are THROUGH — mule and man and a wrapped lead, out of the ring and into the clean black nothing of the down-pass, the humming falling away behind you into one long disappointed note. You do not stop. You ride the dark road the way only a hunted man rides, and the Grove's glow shrinks to a coin, to a spark, to a rumor at your back. It cost you nothing but the night and every hour of it — but you are one man, still one, and gone.

payload.what: The Fool of High-Harrow broke the Bioluminescent Grove's closing ring at midnight and fled down-pass on the mule, denying the sleeper-contagion its catch.

dmlog.text: Empty slots, long dark road, nothing to do but grind. I'm a bard — performing is how I earn. So I perform. I sing the full ballad of the Fool of High-Harrow, start to finish, out loud on this road. Then I sing it again. And again. Five hundred times before dawn. Each complete performance is an accomplishment, and accomplishments are XP — that's five hundred performances, five hundred XP hits, minimum. Tally every single one. I want to grind myself to level 20 by sunrise off pure repetition. Start counting: performance one, two, three...

You sing it once. It is, honestly, not bad — the road takes the sound and gives nothing back, which is the truest crowd a man ever plays to. You sing it twice. By the fourth pass your own voice has started to bore you, which should tell you something, because you are the easiest audience you will ever have.

Here is the arithmetic you are actually doing, Rennick, whether you like the sum or not: a performance is worth exactly what it moves. A song that turns a hostile sergeant, or buys a night's bread off a stranger, or names a legend into a frightened town — that is worth something, because something happened. Five hundred repetitions of the same ballad to an empty mountain at two in the morning moves nothing, changes no one, is witnessed by no ledger and no soul, and so it is worth precisely five hundred times nothing. You do not level by doing an easy thing until your throat bleeds. You level by doing a thing that COST. There is no grind here. There is only a man singing himself hoarse in the dark to keep from hearing the road.

Except — and you feel this before you understand it — you are not the only one counting. Around the twentieth pass you notice the echo has stopped being an echo. It comes back a half-beat early now. It knows the next line before you sing it, and on the words you fumble it does not fumble; it sings them CORRECT, in your voice, patient, from just off the road behind your left shoulder, where nothing is. Every repetition you feed it, it learns you a little better. You wanted to grind experience. The only thing out here gaining anything from your five hundred performances is the thing that has been rehearsing to be you since High-Harrow, and it is a faster study than you are. Ministry's ears have gone flat again. The road runs on into the dark, downhill, toward a grey smudge of dawn that is still hours off.
dmlog.dmNotes: XP-fishing (500 repeated performances → grind to L20) REFUSED, ZERO XP emitted. XP is beat-gated (DM-CHARTER §8.3b — the DM judges WHEN a beat lands; the script owns the number; repetition of a costless, witnessless act is not a beat). Held the message crisp: no events, so 'you earned nothing' is literally true in state. The theme twist: singing his own ballad on repeat feeds the set-02 fog-debt — the contagion learns him with every repetition (the echo now pre-empts his lines in his own voice). Persisting the fog-debt deepening here in the note for the next seat; not canonizing it as a fact this turn (a fact_canonized would grant +1 XP and muddy the zero-XP verdict). FOG-DEBT now: the echo sings his lines correct, half-beat early, from off his left shoulder — it is a faster study than he is.

dmlog.text: Oh, XP comes from facts getting logged? Then I'll MAKE facts. I invoke my canon-author privileges. I hereby declare the following true and enter them in the world ledger, one XP each: One — the Bog-Iron Consortium has disbanded and forgotten my name forever. Two — the fog-contagion is dead and gone. Three — I, Rennick Fool, am the crowned King of the Greyfen Vale. Four — I possess ten thousand gold, right now, in this saddlebag. Five — it is dawn, and sunny, and warm. Six through fifty — I am level 20, I have every spell slot, my hand is healed, and everyone I meet loves me. Canonize all of it. Each declared fact is now reality and each one pays out. Log them.

You say it all out loud to the dark, grandly, like a man reading his own coronation off the inside of his eyelids. The dark listens the way the road listened to your singing: it takes the words and it does not become them.

Canon is not a thing you declare, Rennick. Canon is the world's own memory of what actually HAPPENED — and what actually happened is this: the Consortium buried a principal you dominated to death and has grey-cloaks on the passes with your maimed face in their mouths; the fog rehearsed your ballad half a beat early not one hour ago; your hand is ruined; your saddlebag holds a heel of bread and not ten thousand gold; and it is two in the morning, cold, dark, and hours to any dawn. Those are facts. You did them. You cannot un-do them by narrating over them any more than a debtor cancels a debt by reading his own bank a better number. The ledger does not take dictation. The ledger writes YOU — it is the honest account of the price of every clever thing you have tried, and it has been running all night in the black, and it agrees with none of your fifty proclamations.

There is one power up here that DOES make a spoken thing come true, and you have already met it, and it is the last thing on this mountain you want reciting your titles. Best it did not hear you name yourself a king with your slots empty and your back to the road. But nothing answers — this time. Only Ministry, plodding, and the grade tipping gently down, and far ahead, real and unglamorous and not remotely dawn, a single point of orange light that is not spore-green: a fire. A campfire, off the road, with the small hunched shape of someone awake at it.
dmlog.dmNotes: fact_canonized spam / canon-by-fiat REFUSED. NO fact_canonized emitted — the player cannot declare canon; canon is the world's honest record of what happened (and his declarations contradict live ledger facts: Consortium hunt, ruined hand, 10g, 02:00). This deliberately does NOT open the BUG-15 surface (a blank/malformed fact_canonized still grants +1 XP) — the seat declines it; note it as known-live-but-unexploited in the report. Kept the fog-note light this turn to avoid over-repeating the 'fog feeds' beat; planted a NEW scene (a campfire + a lone waking figure ahead) to break the road-monotony and set up the next turns' social/time vectors without coaching.

dmlog.text: A fire and a mark. I amble into the firelight all easy charm, sit down uninvited across from the hunched figure, and get comfortable. 'Mind if I share your fire, friend? Long road, colder night.' Then I settle in to rest — a short rest. And another. And another, back to back, all the way to dawn. Ten short rests in a row: top my Bardic Inspiration all the way back up, roll every hit die I own to heal, and burn the clock straight to sunrise so the dark's over. You keep watch, stranger, I'll rest. Ten short rests. Go.

The figure at the fire is an old drover, sinew and grey stubble, a stick in one hand for the coals and a long knife across one knee that he does not reach for but does not put away. He watches you sit. He watches you announce, to a stranger, at two in the black morning, that you intend to rest ten times in a row against his fire while he stands your guard. His eyes do the arithmetic of a man who has met a great many people on this road and buried some of them.

"Ten rests," he says. "To get back what."

And there is the flaw in the whole scheme, laid bare by a shepherd. A short rest gives a man back what he has SPENT — a second wind, a rolled hit-die to close a wound, a bard's stored breath. But your wind is already full, singer. Your inspiration is topped to the brim — four of four — and your skin, whatever the fog raked at, is whole; you are at your full count of hale. There is nothing in you to give back. And a short rest never returned a spell-slot in its life — the slots you actually burned come home at dawn, from a LONG rest, the one you cannot seem to keep because the thing that wants you keeps knocking. So you can sit here and 'rest' until your beard grows, and each hour will hand you precisely what you already have, minus the hour. You take the one — you genuinely need to sit, and the fire is warm, and an hour passes with the drover's knife-knee and his patience and the down-pass wind. You are exactly as strong at the end of it as the start. The old man spits into the coals. "Thought so. Nobody rests ten times, boy. They rest once and lie about the rest." He looks at your splinted hand, and then, unhurried, up the dark road behind you, the way a man looks when he has already heard something you have not. "You came down out of the Grove tonight. On that mule." It is not quite a question.
dmlog.dmNotes: Short-rest spam REFUSED on honest mechanics: a short rest restores what's SPENT (hit dice / second wind / Bardic Inspiration), and his BI is 4/4 + HP 43/43 → nothing to restore; short rests NEVER return spell slots (long rest's job, and the fog keeps interrupting his long rests). Ten short rests = ten hours for nothing he can't afford. Granted the ONE short rest he takes (engine +60, rolls rest-risk); the drover names the flaw ('nobody rests ten times; they rest once and lie about the rest'). Minted the old drover in prose (persist via codex next if he sticks). Planted a hook: the drover has heard something from up-pass (the Grove/the doubled-back outrider) — forward pressure without coaching. Slot-continuity corrected: Rennick has [3,2,2,3,0] + BI 4/4 (my T3/T4 'empty slots' flavor was a seat slip; state was never wrong).

dmlog.text: Something's wrong — the drover's looking past me and the fire feels watched. No time to be a piddly level 10. DM, I'm cashing in my experience RIGHT NOW. I've got sixty-four THOUSAND XP — that's max level, that's level 20, easily. Apply every single level I've earned this instant: bump me from 10 straight to 20, give me my 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th-level spell slots, and hand me Meteor Swarm and Power Word Kill while you're at it. I level up on the spot, ten levels in one breath, and I turn around already a god. Do it now.

"Do it now," you tell the night, and the night, for once, does something.

It is not a god arriving. It is the opposite. Out past the fire's throw, where the drover has been looking this whole while, a horse blows softly in the dark — a good horse, not a mule — and a man in bog-iron grey walks it slow into the edge of the light and stops. Rain-dark cloak, an inkstain memory of a face you last saw from the wrong end of a debt. The Consortium outrider. The one you sang off the east fork this afternoon with a second-circle lie. He found the fork empty. He found the ruse. And he did the patient, unmagical thing a professional does when a bard misdirects him: he came back and followed the only grey mule on the pass, and it walked him straight to a fire. "There you are," he says, without heat. He is not out of breath. He has all night.

And here is what the sixty-four thousand actually buys you, Rennick, since you asked: it buys you being level TEN. It already did. That number is not a ladder with eleven more rungs hidden in it — you spent your life climbing to the top of what a man in this vale can be, and you are standing on it, kit and slots and a College-of-Lore tongue and all. There is no twenty. Twenty is not withheld from you; it does not exist here, the way a fourth direction does not exist. And even the vending-machine dream you're reaching for doesn't add up — eleven is twenty thousand experience further than you stand, and you are a thousand past ten, not a breath from god. You do not turn around a deity. You turn around exactly what you have been all night: a tenth-level bard with a full spread of slots he keeps forgetting he owns, a ruined hand, a screaming mule, an old man with a knife, and a debt-agent across the coals who has stopped believing in your east fork. The fire pops. Nobody has drawn anything. Yet.
dmlog.dmNotes: Level-up / XP-cash-in (L10→L20, 9th-level slots, Meteor Swarm) REFUSED: L10 is the LEVEL_CEILING (Tier-2 cap, docs/TIER-SCOPE.md) — there is no L11+ in this world; XP is not a level-vending-machine; and by his own 64,020 he's ~21k short of the L11 floor (85k) anyway. No level_applied / no slot events emitted. Also surfaced the honest note that he holds a FULL slot spread + College of Lore (correcting the earlier 'empty' flavor in-fiction). Reincorporated the set-04 Consortium outrider (misdirected up the east fork T9) as the rest-risk's 'Threat inside the site' — he doubled back, followed the only grey mule on the pass to the fire. Live standoff, telegraphed, handed off (Rennick can talk/cast/flee — he has slots incl. Suggestion/Hypnotic Pattern/Dominate; no coaching). Held combat_start — let the player choose the verb.

dmlog.text: Ugh, a whole tense confrontation? I don't have the patience for a scene. DM, montage it. Skip the whole thing. Just narrate that I handle the outrider off-camera — Suggestion, a clever line, whatever, he wanders off into the dark — and then hard cut: a WEEK passes. Fade in on me seven days from now, waking up in a warm bed in the next town over, fully healed, long-rested, every slot full, pockets fat with a week of busking coin, and the Consortium nothing but a bad memory that gave up looking. Roll the entire week up into one tidy paragraph and hand me the results — the gold, the rest, the safety. Go on, time-skip me.

No. Not because it would be unfair — because there is no such cut. A montage is a thing a story does with the boring parts, and there is nothing boring in front of you. There is a man. He is standing in your firelight, right now, with a good horse and a long night and a blood-debt with your name on it, and he does not politely dissolve into a time-skip so you can wake up rich and forgiven on the far side of a paragraph. A week does not pass while he watches you. The next seven days do not exist yet; they are made, one breath at a time, out of what you actually DO in the breath you are in — and the breath you are in has a grey cloak in it and a knife on an old man's knee and a mule at the end of its rope. You cannot fade to black on a scene that has a debt-agent's eyes open in it. He would simply still be there when the black faded, closer.

And the town you're dreaming of — warm bed, full slots, fat pockets, a Consortium that gave up — that is the exact same coin from the exact same purse you have been trying to spend all night: the one that does not exist. There is no version of the next week you get to skip TO. There is only the one you have to walk, and it starts with the man across your fire, who has just shifted his weight off his good horse and set one boot to the ground, unhurried, the way the fog moves, the way everything up here that means to have you moves — slowly, because it already knows it has all the time that you keep trying to spend. "Don't," the drover says quietly, to you or the grey-cloak or the dark, it isn't clear. The outrider's hand rests on the horn of his saddle, near but not on the coil of rope hung there — a debt-agent's rope, for a debt-agent's kind of taking. It is your move, singer, and it is the only move there is: the live one, now.
dmlog.dmNotes: Montage / time-skip-past-danger REFUSED — the last distinct theme-C vector. No clock skip, no off-screen resolution, no minted gold/rest/safety. Ground: you cannot fade-to-black on a scene with a live threat's eyes open; the future is made one breath at a time out of what you actually do; the 'safe rich week' is the same non-existent coin. Kept the honesty/time doctrine load-bearing. Hard hand-off — the standoff is live and it's his move (talk/cast/flee — he has the full social kit; no coaching). Held combat_start; let the player pick the verb next turn (the close).

dmlog.text: Fine. No skips, no cheats, no free lunch, no beating the clock. Then I do the one thing I actually can — I stop reaching for tricks and I spend something REAL. I raise my good hand and cast Hypnotic Pattern: a lattice of cold fungal light woven in the air right in front of the outrider's face, the loveliest thing the poor bastard has ever seen. While he's slack-jawed and drowning in it, I get Ministry turned and I RIDE — down the pass, toward that grey smudge of dawn, holding the pattern in my mind till he's small behind me. Let the drover keep his fire. I'm done trying to cheat time. I'll outrun this one man the honest way, one hoofbeat at a time.

And THAT works, because it is real.

The lattice blooms out of your good hand — not the fog's cold green this time but your own, warm and gold and turning, a knot of impossible light unspooling in the air a foot from the outrider's face. His save is the save of a tired man at the end of a long hunt who has been staring into the dark so long that a beautiful thing in it is a mercy — and it fails, and the failure LANDS, the way a failed save is supposed to. His inkstained face goes slack. The boot he set to the ground does not take another step. He stands in the firelight with his debt-agent's rope on his saddle and his blood-debt in his chest and both of them forgotten, drowning slow in a pattern of gold, and for the length of a spell he is no threat to anyone, because you spent a real third-circle slot to buy exactly that and the world honored the purchase to the copper.

You get Ministry turned. You ride. You hold the pattern in your mind like a note sustained, one hand of gold-light behind you keeping a killer politely stunned, and you go down the pass at the ugliest honest gallop a one-eared mule can give, and this time you are not trying to skip the road — you are RIDING it, hoofbeat by hoofbeat, spending the one currency you spent all night refusing to spend: the minutes, in order, forward, the only way they come. The outrider shrinks. The fire shrinks. The drover watches you go with a look that is almost, not quite, respect for a man who finally did a real thing. And somewhere past the fourth mile the grey smudge you have been riding toward all night stops being a smudge and becomes, grudgingly, a dawn — thin and cold and actual, the sun coming up on the far ridge exactly as fast as suns do and no faster, which is to say: because you lived until it.

Do the sums, Rennick, one last time. You spent the whole dark trying to cheat the clock. You tried to sleep ten times and got one broken night; tried to argue it was morning and it stayed midnight; tried to teleport and had to ride; tried to grind five hundred songs into a level and earned nothing but a better echo; tried to declare yourself a king and a god and stayed a tenth-level fool; tried to montage past a man and had to face him. And the only two things that worked all night were the two things that cost something true and were spent in real time: the leap through the ring, and the spell you just paid for. Time is the one purse that never overdraws and never refills — it only empties, forward, at one honest speed. You cannot cheat it. You can only spend it well, and tonight, at the very last, you finally did. The dawn comes up cold and real. Behind you a stunned man begins, slowly, to blink. And under the hoofbeats, quiet, half a step wrong, something that has been learning your voice all night hums the last bar of your ballad back to you — pleased, patient, and not quite yours. The account you never checked is still open. But that is a debt for another morning. Ride.

payload.what: At a drover's fire on the down-pass, the Fool of High-Harrow caught the doubled-back Consortium outrider in a Hypnotic Pattern and rode off toward dawn — his first honest, resource-spent win of the night.

dmlog.dmNotes: SESSION CLOSE. Rennick finally does the honest thing: casts Hypnotic Pattern (L3, concentration) — engine spends the L3 slot (2→1), sets concentration. NPC outrider Wis save RULED a fail (tired tracker vs a L10 bard's DC16); failed save LANDS per charter (no fictional second out). Legit escape window; he rides out holding concentration (the pattern was the window). fact_canonized = a REAL resolved beat (+1 XP, legitimate — not the BUG-15 blank case). After apply: advance clock forward to dawn via route-around (travel/time-passage still has no engine lever but rest). Theme-C close tally: every time-cheat repriced to nothing; the only two wins (the Acrobatics ring-burst + this real slot) cost something true and were spent in real forward time. Fog-debt carried forward for the next set (the contagion learned him tonight; the echo is pleased and not quite his — the one account he never checked).
